About I have watched up close where drugs and devices are actually used, and how hospitals buy supplies and hire people. I wrote about the economy and companies on my blog for years before realizing I had left out the field I know best. Mednomics fills that gap. The name joins medicine and economics. I write under a pen name. I want the work judged by its content and evidence, not by a name. Principles Writing principles 01 Public sources only I rely on material anyone can check: news, filings, papers and policy documents. d: Group Purchasing Organization. A purchasing agent that pools buying for many hospitals, negotiates with manufacturers and earns fees. Common in the US.
A questionnaire score for pain, stiffness and function in knee and hip osteoarthritis. Studies often convert it to a 0–100 scale.

An indirect supplier that delivers medical supplies or drugs to hospitals on behalf of manufacturers and distributors. Often partly owned by the hospital foundation or the owner's relatives; its cut is sometimes called a 'toll'.
Buying shares from many shareholders by publicly offering to purchase them outside the market.
A coverage type within national insurance that controls price and use but sets a high co-pay. Raised in the parliamentary audit as a route for obesity drugs.
When a drug is added to the national insurance list and can be prescribed under insurance. A company applies, then goes through assessment and price negotiation.
A deal that transfers rights to a drug to another company in return for an upfront payment and staged milestone payments. Not all of the announced value is guaranteed income.
A rule that punishes both those who offer benefits in return for drug adoption or prescriptions and the doctors or pharmacists who accept them. Introduced in 2010.
The share of a year's net profit paid out as dividends. Paying KRW 50 on KRW 100 of profit is a 50% payout ratio.
An acquisition strategy of adding related businesses to a company you already own, such as buying an intraoral scanner maker for an implant company.
A listed company flagged by the Korea Exchange for failing disclosure duties. Accumulated penalty points can lead to a trading halt or a delisting review.
Care or drugs that national insurance does not cover, so the patient pays in full.
A tax office notice telling a company that a payment is a certain person's income of a certain type and that tax must be withheld. The company then has to withhold accordingly.

The rule that tax follows the real substance of a transaction rather than its name or form. A payment labeled a dividend can be taxed as a kickback if that is what it is, but the tax authority must prove the substance.
Reducing capital by paying shareholders to buy back and cancel shares. When a holding company does it, cash flows back to its owners.
Loans taken to fund buying a company. Private equity commonly stacks such loans on top to buy companies (a leveraged buyout).
A market built on customers effectively guaranteed within a buyer or a group. Critics call it funneling business to affiliates.
Under the amended Medical Devices Act: relatives of a hospital founder within the second degree, holders of more than 50% of shares, or anyone who controls management regardless of shareholding.
A press term for light, non-surgical cosmetic procedures such as Botox, fillers and lifting.

t: EP.01 The purchasing-intermediary ban: hospitals' hidden supply channel
d: University hospitals' purchasing intermediaries are being sold one after another. Is the law closing the channel, or just changing its owner?
x: Two Charts · EP.01 · Hospital money · Oct 31, 2026 · 4 min read The purchasing-intermediary ban: hospitals' hidden supply channel University hospitals' purchasing intermediaries are being sold one after another. Is the law closing the channel, or just changing its owner? Home / Series / The purchasing-intermediary ban: hospitals' hidden supply channel Key points first A purchasing intermediary (gannapsa) is a middleman that delivers medical supplies to hospitals on behalf of manufacturers. The Medical Devices Act amended in December 2025 bans sales to hospitals by related-party dealers. It takes effect on Dec 31, 2027. Related-party test: founder's relatives within the second degree, more than 50% ownership, or controlling influence over management. Hospitals are selling their stakes in intermediaries before it takes effect. The channel is not closing; its owners are changing. The way big hospitals buy supplies is changing. This year, university hospitals' purchasing intermediaries are being sold one after another. Here is why, and how it looks from the operating room. From the stock chart 01 Stents, catheters, artificial joints and surgical tools used in big hospitals' operating rooms mostly do not go straight from the manufacturer to the hospital. 02 They pass through an indirect supplier called a gannapsa, or purchasing intermediary. 03 Each hospital effectively has one designated intermediary, and manufacturers or distributors must go through that door to get products in.

Key points first About 77.5% of a drug wholesaler's shares (57 people) were held by spouses and children of directors of 15 client hospitals. Since 2013 it paid out 49.6% of net profit on average. The tax office treated the dividends as rebates received by nine doctors (other income) and issued a notice of income reclassification. The Tax Tribunal (2025-Seo-3143, late October 2026) overturned it in full. Dividends ranged from KRW 4 to KRW 148 per KRW 100 of drug purchases, not in proportion to prescriptions, and 58% of revenue came from ordinary customers. The ruling concerns the tax assessment only, not whether the Medical Service Act or the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act was broken. In 2025, rebates paid as dividends through a shell company led to criminal charges. There was a drug wholesaler whose shares were more than three-quarters owned by spouses and children of directors of its client hospitals.
